title: His poems
hook: al-Shafi'i also wrote poetry on travel, knowledge and patience

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Risalah, al-Shafi'i's book of method, and your line: method first. Which principle did you pick up, and did it change how you'd decide anything? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-two.

Water that sits still goes bad. Water that runs stays sweet. That line doesn't come from a law book. It comes from a poem, and tradition puts it in the mouth of the same man who wrote the Risalah, the careful book of method from yesterday. Al-Shafi'i, the jurist who built rules for reading rules, also left verses, or verses gathered under his name: on leaving home, on learning, on waiting out hard days. They're short, plain, and easy to learn by heart. Today, the jurist as a poet.
screen: `STILL WATER GOES BAD.` → `RUNNING WATER STAYS SWEET.` → `THE JURIST AS A POET.`

segments.voice: The collection is called the Diwan of al-Shafi'i, a gathering of verses attributed to him. Some readers doubt that every line in it is really his. So, honestly: lines told in his name. Three themes run through them. First, travel. One poem tells the reader to leave home in search of learning and honor: travel, and you'll find something to replace whatever you left behind. Then it reaches for pictures. Still water spoils; running water stays sweet. A lion that never leaves its den never hunts. An arrow that never leaves the bow never hits. Even the sun, the poem says, if it stood still in the sky forever, people would grow tired of it. Second, knowledge. In a short pair of lines, the poet complains to his teacher Waki' about his poor memory. Waki' tells him to leave sins, and explains that knowledge is a light, and the light of God is not given to one who sins. Notice what that does. Study, for him, isn't only hours at a desk. How you live shapes what you can hold. Third, patience. Another poem opens by letting the days do whatever they will, and staying calm when the decree comes down. Hard times pass and good times pass, it says; neither one stays. Put the three side by side and you get a portrait the law books don't give you. The man who argued line by line about evidence and analogy was also someone who left home, struggled to remember, and told himself to wait out the bad days. And the travel lines fit the life this week has followed: Medina with Malik, then Iraq, and at the end Egypt. He did what the poem says.
screen: `THE DIWAN: LINES TOLD IN HIS NAME.` · `TRAVEL: THE LION, THE ARROW, THE SUN.` · `KNOWLEDGE IS A LIGHT.` · `PATIENCE: LET THE DAYS DO AS THEY WILL.`

segments.voice: The practice: read one of his lines. Here is one, in plain English, from the travel poem: travel, and you'll find something to replace what you leave behind. Say it once, slowly. Then ask where in your life the water has gone still. A routine. A room. A habit of thought. You don't have to pack a bag. Travel can be a different route home, a new book, a question asked of someone you don't usually ask. Hold the line and the still place together, and breathe. If you pray, you can ask for a journey that leads somewhere good. The bell holds the time.
His poems. Verses told in al-Shafi'i's name, on travel, on knowledge as a light, and on patience through the days. Today's word.
Your line: travel, and find. Today, take one small journey off your usual track, a new street or a new page, and notice what you find there. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-two.
